newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebel leader arrives back in Lubumbashi.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebel leader arrives back in Lubumbashi.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila returned to his headquarters in southeast Zaire on Friday and rebel officials said he would make an important announcement at a news conference after a cabinet meeting.
Kabila, who had left Cape Town much earlier on Friday by plane after talks with South Africa President Nelson Mandela, made no comment as he arrived in Zaire's second city Lubumbashi.
Rebel officials said he went straight into a meeting of his "cabinet" and would make an important announcement at a news conference later on Friday. They declined to give any details.
It was unclear where Kabila had gone during the long gap between when he left Cape Town and when he landed in Lubumbashi.
Kabila, who in October launched the rebellion against Mobutu that has taken his forces almost to Kinshasa, returned after a government announcement that President Mobutu Sese Seko gave up power.

But a government statement said he would retain the title of president. He had earlier flown to his northern jungle palace at Gbadolite on Friday from the capital Kinshasa, triggering intense speculation that he had started a journey into exile.

Zairean government spokesman Kin-Kiey Mulumba announced Mobutu was giving up his powers at a Kinshasa news conference after a cabinet meeting. But he said that Mobutu's emergency rule prime minister, Geneval Likulia Bolongo, was now in charge.
Kisangani Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo, a key player early in Zaire's democratic transition, would negotiate with Kabila's rebels on a new transitional government and elections, Kin-Kiey said.
"The president...has ceased all intervention in the affairs of the state," Kin-Kiey said. Kabila has long demanded Mobutu step down but it was unclear if he would agree to negotiate with Monsengwo.

Kabila's rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire had threatened to attack Kinshasa if Monsengwo returned to Kinshasa to take up the position of speaker of Zaire's transitional parliament earlier this month.

"If the parties to the conflict, in particular the rebel alliance, act in good faith, the president's important decision to stand aside, coupled with the constraints which the constitution imposes...will allow us to find a satisfactory compromise between the positions of the belligerents," Kin-Kiey said.

Kabila on Thursday agreed to a request from Mandela to give Mobutu until Monday to study proposals for a peaceful handover of power in Africa's third largest country. He declined to say if he would halt the rebel advance on the country's capital.
Kabila, 56, has demanded an immediate transfer of power to his rebel alliance and had said that Mobutu would be hunted down if he remained in Kinshasa when the rebel forces arrived.
